explainBack.question: Why might Muse send a calendar-style reply on your behalf one day without asking, after prompting you for approval the first time?
explainBack.answer: Because approval is not a per-action ritual but a scoped grant. The first time, the outside control found no matching permission for that connected service, so it stopped the action and asked you; you may have chosen a permanent or task-scoped grant. Afterwards, any proposed action that fits exactly inside that granted scope — or that is read-only or judged low-risk — is allowed through to the internet without interruption. The agent never decides this itself; the separate control compares each proposal against your standing grant.
explainBack.expectedEvidence: P005 (control outside the agent checks whether a proposed action fits the permission before letting it reach the internet) and P006 (grant types include permanent; previously allowed, read-only or low-risk actions may proceed without interruption).
explainBack.assessment: The article fully supports this causal answer: both the scope-matching step and the uninterrupted-action condition are explicit, so a reader can predict silent actions rather than being surprised by them.

unseenTransfer.scenario: A reader connects Muse to her broadband provider's account portal and asks it to negotiate a lower monthly bill, something the article never discusses. Muse reads her current plan, chats with the provider's retention bot overnight while her phone is off, and reaches a moment where accepting the new 12-month contract would commit her to a fee.
unseenTransfer.question: Using only this article's mechanism, what should she expect at each step, and does today's setup keep this negotiation private from Meta?
unseenTransfer.answer: Reading her plan details can proceed without interruption once she granted read access, because read-only and previously allowed actions skip fresh prompts (P006). The overnight work matches Meta's claim that Muse continues after the app closes (P003). But accepting the contract is a consequential action on a connected service: the control outside the agent should find no standing grant covering it and stop to ask her, and she can prefer a one-time grant so no permanent contract-signing power lingers (P005, P006, P009). Afterwards she can inspect every step in the audit trail. On privacy: no — today's workspace only separates her from other users; Meta may still access the data to operate, support or secure the service, and the negotiation transcript may feed model training unless she opted out. The version where even Meta cannot see it is a promise still with trusted testers (P008).
unseenTransfer.expectedEvidence: P005–P006 for scope-checked approval and uninterrupted low-risk reads, P003 for background continuation, P008 for current Meta access versus the future encrypted workspace, P009 for one-time grants and the audit trail.
unseenTransfer.assessment: The mechanism transfers cleanly to this new situation with no gaps: the article gives a reader everything needed to predict prompts, choose grant scope, and correctly judge today's privacy boundary.

learningDisposition.rationale: All eleven outcomes and four news checks pass, and all twenty-four failure families are clear with specific passage grounding; no failed or uncertain assessment exists in the reader part.

reader.summary: A tight, well-scoped news article that makes the agent-to-permission-to-service chain genuinely legible: the agent proposes, a control outside it checks the grant scope, and only matching actions reach the connected service. It cleanly separates today's protections (user isolation, Meta operational access, training default) from the promised user-key-encrypted workspace still in trusted testing, ends on a specific access decision, and passes every outcome and news check with no failure family present.
